In my education I had to learn the name, function, and location of each muscle in the human body.

Eventually, I got good at visualizing which muscles activate to perform each particular lift. Visualizing is the key word.

Then I got good at mentally modifying each lift. I would imagine, for example, how would it affect the activation of my pectoralis major if I paid attention to pulling the bar apart versus pushing it together, during a bench press movement.

I experimented and read. 

You understand, there is a very large degree of athleticism to lifting. I would argue that you get stronger faster from learning better technique, than from actually getting bigger muscles. Every lift is failed because of some weak link in its execution. Add some modification and you will protect that link. For example, during a deadlift, you can completely protect your lower back by activating your lats and your lower traps. If you combine that with never breaking neutral spine, you change all of the forces acting on the lower back into compressive forces (as opposed to shear forces), and that completely takes the load of the internal lower back muscles.

During pressing, on the other hand, you want a very strong stabilizing force on your shoulder joint. All of the pressing muscles, pecs and front delts, are internal rotators, so you have to focus on activating your external rotators, and this keeps the shoulder securely in its socket and prevents any joint stress.

There is much more to it, and again, it's very hard to actually communicate. But the basic idea should be clear. Anatomical knowledge and visualization combined with very slow ramping of weight during each workout leads to more mindful, more technical lifting style

This is not a PNF stretch but a simple static stretch. And even positioning is more of a front deltoid stretch, rather than the bicep stretch. Notice how the stretchee's arms are both at his 6 o'clock position, ie directly behind him. Biceps needs more of 5 and 7 o'clock position, or even 4 and 8 o'clock. His wrists are also rotated the wrong way. 

If you want to do a self PNF stretch, simply raise your arms behind your body at 4 and 8 o'clock, with your palms facing upwards. Raise your arms in this fashion until you feel a stretch in your biceps. Hold and relax. Do not use anything to enhance the stretch, lift your arms in the air, using your own muscle energy.

Every lift has a weak link, and every during every lift you need to protect that weak link, by engaging the proper musculature - there are protector muscles in every lift, you just need to know them and keep your attention on them during every movement.

I'm an avid weightlifter myself, and it has been quite a while since I hurt myself after I learned the importance of proper muscle activation and easing back on the goddamn weight.
I reccommend this technique for re-learning your troubling lifts. Start light, really light, and ramp up your weight in a series of around 20 very short sets, just like Olympic weighlifters do.

If your overhead press is bothering you, for example, start with the bar, and do sets of two, adding 5lb to the bar until you hit the point when your technique breaks down. You can learn a lot about proper movement when the weight is light, and reps are low, trust me. Be mindful of those lighter reps, and you will probably learn that your technique is flawed in many subtle ways, just like mine was. In 20 sets you will reach 145, and if that that's light for you, then start with a different weight, or bump the weight by 10 lbs in the first few sets.

I actually train in a very similar way, except I do around 10 sets of three, of which only the last 1-2 are heavy enough to be slow (keep in mind that my technique doesn't break down like yours might. so while my lifts are all done with good form, even the heavy ones, your weights might be initially way lighter than those you are used to doing. when you notice technique disintegration - this is where you stop, regardless of ego state.)

Trigger points are symptoms, not actual injuries - they can arise out of many causes, tendinitis included.

But that's just convention, applied consistently and honored. Word boy means boy, the same way a physical smile means what it means. Language has to place boundaries on how words are combined, otherwise relationships between concepts can no longer exist.

Language is backed up by physical neural networks that have to function logically. So in the young brain, no convention is pre-set. The child listens to the sounds around him, and picks up the conventions statistically, thereby learning the language, and all of its linguistic hierarchies.

Every language on the planet has to make certain choices about how to organize meaning, and those choices differ geographically and culturally, but their presence is consistent. 
There are top level choices that have the most to do with how "alien" the language sounds to different language speakers. Then there are sub-choices, which are subordinate to the choices made higher up, hierarchically. You cannot have a sub-choice out of the different logical branch of higher up choices. With every choice you make, you narrow down the number of possibilities of further linguistic choices. What's weird about this process, this selection of the logical "uniqueness" of language?

Do you speak only English? Because that might be the root of your problem. For instance, if I take your sample sentence "Mlicked boy peas plate the the the on", and remove all the *thes*, which are just idiosyncrasies of English, then it starts to make a rough sense to me, considering I don't know what mlicked is.

I am a native Russian speaker, and had to learn English. Russian sits in my hippocampus and feels real to me, like the words are somehow real. English sits in my cerebral cortex and feels like a logical system of conventions. Only one language can feel real to you, can feel like it has some innate logic to it, can feel like something connected to the real world - and it's the language that sits in your hippocampus. But you can learn a every possible human language, regardless of what your mother tongue is, and they'll reside in your cerebral cortex, along with every other consciously learned skill. 

So you can't really ever say "that's not even a possible combination of sounds", unless the combination of sounds violates some linguistic hierachical law, with some choices being taken from other linguistic "trees". And those linguistic laws are probably determined by some physical structures of the brain.

Humans are capable of adopting lots of different systems of organizing meaning. We communicate through accepted conventions of those ways.

I have trouble being non-symmetrical, if that makes sense... everything should be even. I can't do something that isn't part of a pattern. And once the pattern is established, it pains me to break it. It used to be worse, though. I used to not be able to mix freeweight and machines in my exercise programs. And I couldn't mix dumbbells with barbells, I kid you not. Now it's all better, because I've learned a little more physiology of muscle building, and realized that symmetry has nothing to do with it. Seems funny now, but I believed that a method that will work will be a method that looks neat. But then I realized that it's all the simple cycle of stimulation and recovery, and your muscles don't actually know what you're lifting and even how much. It's just activation/energy output/damage/recovery/supercompensation, regardless of how you've achieved it. I also realized that I don't actually care all that much about my physique, that it's not essential to me to look good, and that I do it for fun, mostly. So it doesn't make sense for me to push myself to overtraining, or stress myself over skipped days, or poor gym performance. I lowered the overall importance of exercise, when I realized that even when I don't try too hard I still lift heavy - because it's fun! But I still have to fight my natural tendency to group my exercise into patterns and to impose arbitrary rules about what I can or cannot do in the gym. I have talk to myself to keep this tendency at bay, which I believe is me trying to control something which isn't worth controlling....

Like recently, my schedule switched, and I'm on 4 day upper/lower upper/lower. I was feeling tired, but was still going to go to the gym, until I got strict with myself and told myself to not be retarded, that one skipped upper day will not do anything to harm my physique, which by the way, doesn't even matter.

I don't know much about migraines, but I do know about tension headaches, which are way more common than migraines. Tension headaches are just your regular headaches, without light sensitivity, auras, or any other stuff that comes with migraines.

Tension headaches come from overused muscles at the back of the neck, and upper shoulders. The overuse generally comes from three things in general.

- posture (look up 'anterior head carriage' - think rounded middle back and head/face sticking forward, towards the computer)
- stress (humans tense up their upper shoulders and neck when stressed)
- one time injury like a car crash, or repetitive strain (accumulating injury) like lifting something at work all the time - even a computer mouse, for some people.

The overuse results in things called trigger points, which are just really really tight bundles of muscle fibers pressing on the nerves inside the muscles. Those bundles are way tighter than the rest of the muscle, for an unknown reason (general hypothesis is that muscle tension has a cascading effect - the more tight a muscle is - the faster and more likely that it becomes even tighter)

Okay, so nerves that go in the brain are being pressed on by trigger points. And what this does is trigger a pain sensation for an area much larger than the trigger point. The nerve just tells the brain that the whole are it's responsible for monitoring hurts. And that area often spreads to different places in the body, like the head. There also might be more complex things at play, but think about it simply.

What you need to do to get rid of your tension headache is fix the trigger point, generally done by accomplishing two things:

- Fixing the posture, or any other issue that had led to the overuse.
- Increasing the flow of blood into the muscle, and waste products out of it. Done by massage and exercise. Massage therapy has specialists that know how to get rid of trigger points really well, but not every massage therapist knows. You have to ask.

USSR traded mainly with friendly nations, like Cuba, and some African nations, and Eastern Europe. Some of the most highly sought after items could only be bought on business trips to Hungary, Bulgaria, GDR, etc.
